title: 2 Chronicles 1:1–13
context: Solomon, now firmly established, gathers Israel and goes to the high place at Gibeon. The Chronicler gives a reason 1 Kings 3 states only in part: “God’s Tent of Meeting was there, which the LORD’s servant Moses had made in the wilderness,” and the bronze altar of Bezalel stood before the LORD’s tabernacle. The ark, however, was in the tent David had pitched in Jerusalem. Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings, and that night God appears and tells him to ask. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to judge the people; God grants that gift and adds riches, wealth, and honor. The gift of wisdom is shared ground with 1 Kings 3:5–15. The two accounts should be named as parallels and not forced into one form. In 1 Kings 3:2–4 the people and Solomon sacrifice at the high places because the temple is not yet built, and Gibeon is called “the great high place.” Those notes already record some unease about the high places and note that Chronicles supplies the tent and the altar, a fact many readers take as explaining why this worship is told as it is, though the matter is discussed rather than settled. 1 Kings 3:5 calls the appearance a dream; this chapter says, “That night, God appeared to Solomon”, without using the word dream. Both traditions read the unit as the LORD establishing Solomon and giving him wisdom for the people, without inventing a party contrast over Gibeon or over the form of the appearance.

verses.text: Solomon the son of David was firmly established in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him, and made him exceedingly great.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Solomon the son of David was firmly established in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him, and made him exceedingly great.” The book opens with Solomon already set in place, and with the LORD’s presence as the reason for his greatness. The wording is close to the close of 1 Kings 2, where the kingdom is established in Solomon’s hand, but this verse makes the LORD’s being with him explicit.

Arminian readers hear a real establishing at the start of the reign, the LORD with David’s son, not a later achievement Solomon first earns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the LORD’s initiative. He is with Solomon and makes him exceedingly great, the ground on which the assembly, the journey to Gibeon, and the gift of wisdom will stand.

Both traditions take the opening as shared confession: the kingdom is the LORD’s gift to David’s son.

verses.text: Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every prince in all Israel, the heads of the fathers’ households.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon speaks to all Israel: captains, judges, princes, and the heads of the fathers’ households. The Chronicler gathers a wide assembly before the journey to Gibeon, a public setting 1 Kings 3 does not describe in the same way.

Arminian readers take the summons as a real act of leadership. The king does not go to Gibeon alone; the heads of the people are called to go with him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a national scene, not a private errand. All Israel is addressed, and the next verse will take the assembly to Gibeon.

Both traditions read the verse as the Chronicler’s way of placing the coming worship and the coming gift in the sight of the people.

verses.text: Then Solomon, and all the assembly with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon; for God’s Tent of Meeting was there, which the LORD’s servant Moses had made in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon and all the assembly go to “the high place that was at Gibeon; for God’s Tent of Meeting was there, which the LORD’s servant Moses had made in the wilderness.” 1 Kings 3:4 calls Gibeon the great high place and records the same journey to sacrifice. This verse names the Tent as the reason they go there. The two descriptions should stand side by side, not be forced into one explanation of the high place.

Arminian readers hear a real assembly at a real site, the Mosaic Tent still at Gibeon, which the already drafted 1 Kings 3 notes also mention as Chronicles’ added notice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers keep the same restraint. Gibeon is a high place, and it is also the place of the Tent of Meeting in this book. The tension is to be named, not resolved by a theory the verse does not give.

Both traditions refuse to turn the site into a type, and they do not invent a party contrast over it.

verses.text: But David had brought God’s ark up from Kiriath Jearim to the place that David had prepared for it; for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But David had brought God’s ark up from Kiriath Jearim to the place that David had prepared for it; for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem.” The Tent of Meeting is at Gibeon; the ark is in Jerusalem. The Chronicler will not let the reader confuse the two. The earlier story of the ark’s coming up is assumed, not retold.

Arminian readers take the contrast as a historical fact of the period before the temple: the ark and the Mosaic Tent are not yet in one house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same careful distinction. David has already prepared a place in Jerusalem, and the later temple will gather what is now divided.

Both traditions read the verse as explanation, not as a slight against Gibeon or against the coming visit there.

verses.text: Moreover the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made was there before the LORD’s tabernacle; and Solomon and the assembly were seeking counsel there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The bronze altar that Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, had made “was there before the LORD’s tabernacle; and Solomon and the assembly were seeking counsel there.” The altar of Exodus is located at Gibeon with the tabernacle. 1 Kings 3:4 speaks of the altar at the great high place without naming Bezalel. The difference of detail should be reported, not erased.

Arminian readers take the seeking of counsel at that altar as genuine worship, the assembly inquiring at the place the Tent and the altar still occupied.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the parallel and the added names. Bezalel’s altar stands before the tabernacle, and Solomon and the assembly seek counsel there.

Both traditions keep the verse as a worship scene, consistent with the 1 Kings 3 notes that treat the offerings as sincere, while still leaving the high-place question discussed rather than settled.

verses.text: Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before the LORD, which was at the Tent of Meeting, and offered one thousand burnt offerings on it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the LORD at the Tent of Meeting “and offered one thousand burnt offerings on it.” The number matches 1 Kings 3:4, “Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.” The offering is the same scale in both books.

Arminian readers hear extravagant, public devotion at the start of the reign, a real act of worship and not a mere preface to a private dream.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the thousand offerings as the shared report of the two accounts. The next verse will tell what happened that night.

Both traditions refuse to minimize the sacrifice or to turn the number into a symbol.

verses.text: That night, God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Ask for what you want me to give you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
That night, God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Ask for what you want me to give you.” The invitation matches the substance of 1 Kings 3:5, where the LORD appears at Gibeon in a dream by night. This verse says God appeared that night and does not use the word dream. The two forms should be named, not forced into one description.

Arminian readers hear a genuine invitation. Solomon is asked what he wants, and his answer will matter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that God appears and offers a gift, as in 1 Kings 3:5. The initiative is the LORD’s, whether or not this chapter uses the word dream.

Both traditions take the gift of wisdom as shared ground: it is God’s gift, Solomon asks in order to judge the people, and the Chronicler, like 1 Kings 3, presents that request as the right one.

verses.text: Solomon said to God, “You have shown great loving kindness to David my father, and have made me king in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon answers, “You have shown great loving kindness to David my father, and have made me king in his place.” He begins, as in 1 Kings 3:6, with God’s kindness to David and with his own place on the throne, though the wording is shorter here and does not repeat David’s walk in the same detail.

Arminian readers hear a real gratitude. The kingship is received as a gift in David’s place, not claimed as Solomon’s achievement.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from God’s loving kindness to David, the same ground as 1 Kings 3:6. The son sits because of what God has shown the father.

Both traditions take the opening of the prayer as shared confession, not as a party argument about the covenant.

verses.text: Now, LORD God, let your promise to David my father be established; for you have made me king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude.
verses.arminianNotes:
He continues, “Now, LORD God, let your promise to David my father be established; for you have made me king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude.” The prayer appeals to the promise to David and to the size of the people, language that recalls the older promises of a multitude, without this verse quoting them at length.

Arminian readers hear Solomon holding God to a promise already given, and asking that it be established in his own reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same appeal. The promise to David is the ground, and the people are already like the dust of the earth in multitude.

Both traditions read the verse as a prayer that God’s word to David would stand, the setting for the request that follows.

verses.text: Now give me wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people; for who can judge this great people of yours?”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now give me wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people; for who can judge this great people of yours?” The request matches the heart of 1 Kings 3:9, an understanding to judge the people, though 1 Kings asks for an understanding heart to discern good and evil, and this verse asks for wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in. The two wordings should stand as they are.

Arminian readers hear a request aimed at the people, not at private gain. Solomon asks for what the task requires.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see a need only God can meet. The people are “this great people of yours”, and wisdom is asked so that the king may serve them.

Both traditions take the gift of wisdom as shared ground: it is God’s gift, Solomon asks in order to judge the people, and the Chronicler, like 1 Kings 3, presents that request as the right one.

verses.text: God said to Solomon, “Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked riches, wealth, honor, or the life of those who hate you, nor yet have you asked for long life; but have asked for wisdom and knowledge for yourself, that you may judge my people, over whom I have made you king,
verses.arminianNotes:
God answers that because this was in Solomon’s heart, he has not asked riches, wealth, honor, the life of those who hate him, or long life, but wisdom and knowledge in order to judge the people. The list of things not asked is close to 1 Kings 3:11, with small differences of wording. The commendation falls on the request itself.

Arminian readers hear God responding to what was truly in the king’s heart, a real evaluation of the request.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that God himself names the motive and grants what serves the people he has set under Solomon.

Both traditions take the gift of wisdom as shared ground: it is God’s gift, Solomon asks in order to judge the people, and the Chronicler, like 1 Kings 3, presents that request as the right one.

verses.text: therefore wisdom and knowledge is granted to you. I will give you riches, wealth, and honor, such as none of the kings have had who have been before you, and none after you will have.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“therefore wisdom and knowledge is granted to you. I will give you riches, wealth, and honor, such as none of the kings have had who have been before you, and none after you will have.” The gift of wisdom is granted, and unasked riches and honor are added, as in 1 Kings 3:12–13. This verse does not add the conditional promise of long life found in 1 Kings 3:14. That difference should be named, not filled in from the other book.

Arminian readers receive wisdom and knowledge as a real grant, and the added gifts as generosity, without importing the missing condition as if it had been spoken here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the two accounts side by side. Wisdom is given; riches and honor are added; the long-life condition of 1 Kings 3:14 is not restated in this answer.

Both traditions take the gift of wisdom as shared ground: it is God’s gift, Solomon asks in order to judge the people, and the Chronicler, like 1 Kings 3, presents that request as the right one.

verses.text: So Solomon came from the high place that was at Gibeon, from before the Tent of Meeting, to Jerusalem; and he reigned over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon comes “from the high place that was at Gibeon, from before the Tent of Meeting, to Jerusalem; and he reigned over Israel.” 1 Kings 3:15 has him wake from a dream, go to Jerusalem, and stand before the ark with offerings and a feast. This close names Gibeon, the Tent, and the return to reign, and does not mention the ark or the feast. The endings differ and should not be forced together.

Arminian readers take the return as the start of the public reign after the gift, a historical close of the Gibeon scene.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the two endings unmerged. He leaves the Tent at Gibeon and reigns in Jerusalem, the wisdom already granted.

Both traditions close the unit on that shared gift and that return, without a contrast over the missing details of 1 Kings 3:15.
